utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. I do understand that the present witness is the last witness available for today. If I look at our schedule, tomorrow's witness should be easily concluded tomorrow as well. I see even a very precise estimate of the Prosecution; one hour and 25 minutes, not one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After that witness tomorrow, is the next witness ready or is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The next witness is coming on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Radulj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radulj.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, we left it off with the questions concerning your new job; i.e., when you became deputy military prosecutor. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, in October 1993 when you joined the Military Prosecutor's Office, how many prosecutors were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was the chief prosecutor, there were three deputies, and I came as a fourth deputy. Only a month later one of the colleagues left. I believe that he went to Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the military prosecutor when you were his deputy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Srboljub Jovicinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the territorial competence of the Military Prosecutor's Office where you started working? What area did your Military Prosecutor's Office cover?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Military Prosecutor's Office in Banja Luka covered the zones of responsibility of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps. In geographical terms, that would be the line from Brcko to Ozren and Doboj and then further on to Mount Vlasic, Kupres, Grahovo, all the way up to Novi Grad in the direction of Bihac. The northern boundary of that territory, of course, would be the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was your subject jurisdiction? What did you, as a military prosecutor, do for the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject jurisdiction of the military prosecutor's office and of the military court was to process all the crimes that were committed by members of the VRS, either active or reserve troops while they served in the military. Serving in the military also implied their travel from the unit to their homes, because the units were providing transportation for their troops when they travelled from the line to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A very practical question: A military conscript who was on leave and who was at home and who committed a crime, who would have the jurisdiction to process and bring charges against such a person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when a member of the armed forces was on leave, in that case he was considered to be a civilian; i.e., it was a civilian court or a civilian prosecutor's office that would have been in charge of the crimes committed by such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now on to something different. If a civilian who was not engaged in any of the units of the VRS committed a crime that had something to do with the military - i.e., spying or stealing military property or any other type of misdemeanour, a crime, for example, sabotage, something that had to do with the army - who would be in charge of processing such a person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me expand a little in order to answer your question. At that time, we applied the criminal code of the SFRY and the criminal code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the criminal code of the SFRY, there were crimes, I believe under Chapter 15 or 20, I'm not sure, so crimes against armed forces and security and safety. If anybody, a civilian or a member of the military, committed a crime against the security of the state or the military, they would be charged by the military prosecutor's office and they would be tried by a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question about your jurisdiction. If a crime was committed and if it didn't fell under the chapter of crimes against the military and safety, and if such a crime was committed by an active or reserve police officer, who would be in charge of processing such a crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember whether we had any such cases, but I believe that the law was very clear in that respect. It says that everybody who committed such a crime, irrespective of their status, and if a crime was against safety, security, and armed forces, such crimes would be processed by a military court which had the jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If such a person - i.e., a policeman - committed a conventional crime such as theft, robbery, murder, who would be in charge of processing such a policeman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a case, it would be regular - i.e., civilian courts - that would process such a policeman because those crimes are not considered to have been committed against the military or the safety and security of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within the context of questions of subject matter jurisdiction, the military prosecutor's office that you worked for, were you in charge of processing all the crimes, irrespective of their gravity and the punishment provided for them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me take things step by step. The military judiciary and the military prosecutor's office, when it came to first instance procedures, did you prosecute all the crimes irrespective of their gravity and the punishments and sentences provided for them, or was there a second instance as well, or a different instance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I think I've understood your question. Since there were first instance courts, and there was also a supreme military court, the first instance courts and the prosecutor's office were in charge of all the cases of crimes, irrespective of the sentence provided for them. Only the supreme court could act as a second instance court in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, in the answer there is a switch from competence of the prosecutor and the competence of the court. To say the prosecutor would prosecute whatever before the first instance but the supreme court ... So we should clearly distinguish between the competence and jurisdiction of the prosecutor's office and of the court's and that's a bit chaotic in your answer. So if you would please explain, that would be appreciated. Perhaps the most question then is: Was your office, your prosecutorial office, also competent to prosecute the cases in second instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Shall I answer? The prosecutor was in charge of all the cases, irrespective of the sentencing. When it came to the second instance proceedings, the prosecutor filed appeals against the decisions of the first instance court, and that was the only role when it came to the second instance decision-making; i.e., filing appeals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if the convicted person or accused, whatever you call him, would file an appeal, would you then also further prosecute that person before the appellate court, the supreme court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what happened. If the accused was not satisfied with the sentence, he had the right to appeal to the supreme military court. When the supreme military court received such an appeal, it informed the prosecutor's office about that appeal having been filed. And then the prosecutor had the right to issue a written response to such an appeal. Such a response was then considered by the supreme court and made its final decision accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So where you earlier said that the only role was where the prosecutor appealed, the role was a bit more extensive because you were involved in appeal proceedings as well, if the accused or the convicted person had appealed the judgement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Only those of us who were not members of the military judiciary would like to know where was the military prosecutor's office located at the time in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The full title of the institution was the Prosecutor's Office of the Army of Republika Srpska and its seat was in Han Pijesak. Towards the end of the war, it was moved to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where was the seat of the supreme military court which dealt with cases as a second instance institution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seat of the supreme military court was first in Han Pijesak as well and later it was moved to Zvornik. These two institutions have always occupied the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were your conditions of work like? When I say "your conditions of work," I mean the premises, the staffing, the equipment capabilities.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, our conditions were very dire. And that's an understatement. There were not enough professionals or administrative staff. We had old mechanical typewriters so that it took a typist almost half an hour to type a single page. The premises were inadequate. There was not enough room. There were very frequent electricity outages, and the chief prosecutor used an old Golf I vehicle for which, more often than not, he didn't even have enough petrol. The seat was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, was there a facility that was used to detain those persons who had to be remanded in custody?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the barracks Mali Logor, that was the name of the barracks, there was a military investigation prison, VIZ, where suspects were kept, suspects that were dealt with by the military judiciary and the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could I ask for clarification, Mr. Stojanovic. Sir, at page 7, line 18, you are recorded as saying: "The seat was in Banja Luka." The seat of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The seat of the basic military prosecutor's office for the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps where I worked. Because the question pertained to conditions of work in the 1st and 2nd -- or rather, the prosecutor's office where I worked. I think that I was specific on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Earlier you told us that the prosecutor's office were seated first in Han Pijesak and then later in Zvornik. That's why I'm asking the question now about Banja Luka. Where does Banja Luka come in? Because you haven't told us before that the prosecutor's seat was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I will explain in detail. There were first instance prosecutor's offices that covered the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. There was a prosecutor's office in Bijeljina that covered the area of eastern Bosnia. Then there was a prosecutor's office at Sokolac for the area of the Sarajevo and Romanija regions, and the prosecutor's office in Bileca for the area of the Bileca Corps. These were first instance organs. The Defence counsel asked me where the seat was of the supreme military court and prosecutor's office. So this was the second instance organ. The military prosecutor's office of Republika Srpska had its seat in Han Pijesak. Later on, they were moved to Zvornik. So these are second instance organs for these two institutions. That is why I mentioned Han Pijesak and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Next question that I actually started already: According to the solutions provided for then in the Law on Criminal Procedure, within the system, who was in charge of carrying out investigations against suspects, persons suspected of having committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Law on Criminal Procedure that was in force then, the investigation was carried out by the court; or rather, the investigating judge of the military court, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the law, who submits a request for carrying out an investigation and who prosecutes suspects and indictees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law that was in force then, the military prosecutor's office had the following authority: After a criminal report was filed and if there are reasonable grounds to suspect that a person had committed a crime, within the shortest period of time it was their duty to submit a request to the investigating judge of the military court to carry out an investigation. After the investigation, his duty is to return the case to the prosecutor in charge for taking further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question in this regard. According to the law then, within this system, who was in charge of making proposals and who was in charge of remanding persons into custody or releasing them from custody?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the law, the military prosecutor was supposed to make proposals related to detention; however, it is also the duty of the court to remand persons into custody if the crime involved is such that the law stipulates that the envisaged sentence for the commission of such a crime is ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say ten years, do you mean as a minimal sentence or as a possible sentence? I'm speaking of obligatory detention now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, after all this time, I cannot be sure. I think that it was at least ten years in prison. I cannot be certain, but I think it was ten years and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I fully understand. We've been through so many amendments to all these laws. Now, in the system of the prosecutor's office, who is the one who says -- according to the law, who says in the system, "This is a war crime" or "No, this is homicide" or "This is aggravated robbery" or "No, this is robbery"? So who qualifies the crime committed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system of work in the military prosecutor's office was as follows: The chief prosecutor would receive all the cases, and I remember very well on the front page of the document involved he would qualify the crime, is it homicide, is it evasion of military obligation, or whatever else. Then we, as deputies, desk officers, act on the basis of instructions issued by the chief prosecutor. However, at the time the judge was not bound by what the prosecutor had said. It is the facts of the case that guide the judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my next question. When you say that the judge is not bound by this, rather, the judge is only guided by the facts of the case, my question is as follows: According to the law then, did the court have the possibility to look at the same facts but to qualify the crime in different terms from a legal point of view?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The court did have that right. And, in practice, there were cases when the court would say that the crime committed was not as serious as what the prosecutor had originally charged. Also, the reverse was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your work, you, as deputy prosecutor, were you ever subjected to any kind of pressure with regard to the prosecution of perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No pressure whatsoever. Of course, I followed the orders of my superior, the chief prosecutor, and I acted on the basis of his instructions and guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You as an organ of the military judiciary - that is to say, as the military prosecutor's office - were you duty-bound to submit reports to someone and, if so, to who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our work was subject to checks, of course, and I know that the chief prosecutor often went to attend meetings at corps commands and the commands of other units where he would report on the work of the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When qualifying certain crimes, did you as deputy prosecutor have situations when you were pressured to do something which was the complete opposite of what your own opinion was with regard to a particular crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No pressure was exerted. But I don't think that the prosecutor's office was submitted to pressure either, because the prosecutor was a military professional anyway, and he had such a personality that it was very difficult to affect him in any way. We, his co-workers, thought, and think to this day, that he was a professional, even more strict than necessary. I would even say that he's a man who was a bit career-driven too, and influenced others, as a matter of fact, wanting to have matters resolved in a lawful way. So it was very hard to exercise any kind of influence over him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As deputy prosecutor, and later on as a military prosecutor yourself, did you have any problems with evidence, collecting evidence, access to possible crime scenes, carrying out on-site investigations, getting witnesses who would be relevant in supporting the indictment, also issuing subpoenas? So I'm referring to procedural matters. Did you have any difficulties in your work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, I came to the military prosecutor's office towards the end of 1993. The situation was a bit better then than it had been during 1992. The problem then was reaching the scene, collecting evidence, the impossibility of reaching witnesses, precisely because we did not have a vehicle to reach the scene. As I said, the area is from Brcko to Bihac. At any rate, everything depended on what the military police and security organs would obtain and submit to the prosecutor's office. Later, everything that was not done at first would subsequently be done by the investigating judge who was in charge of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the law that was in force then, speaking in terms of procedure, how much time could a suspect or indictee spend in detention in the investigation prison?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: In the military prosecutor's office, we had a lot of problems there. Usually, the police would bring in a certain person, and such a person would be remanded in custody for two days. The prosecutor's office was duty-bound within those two days to prepare the relevant evidence and file a request for carrying out an investigation and make a proposal on the extension of custody, first of all, for one month. During this very short period of time, in view of the fact that we did not have sufficient resources, including human resources, we sometimes had to work day and night so that we could get things done on time. May I mention that we usually worked from 7.00 to 7.00. There were no real working hours. Also, it depended on whether we had electricity. So if we would manage to submit a request for carrying out an investigation, the person who was in detention could remain in detention until the end of the investigation, but the maximum period was six months. However, if the investigating judge would not complete the investigation, that person, regardless of the crime involved, would have to be released from custody on the basis of the law. Even if the prosecutor's office were to ask for an extension of detention, the court would release them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us now, specifically, you as deputy military prosecutor in that period, if you still remember, did you have any situations when you would charge Serbs or indict persons of Serb ethnicity and the injured party would be a person or persons of non-Serb ethnicity, irrespective of the crime involved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. Serbs committed crimes against non-Serbs and were charged for them. It's hard for me to remember all such cases, but I do remember one which was very hard. In any case, a non-Serb was murdered for the gain of some petty cash, and that Serb who committed the murder was sentenced to 12 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were other cases of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, that one case you remember, was that murder committed in the context of combat or in context of any military activity, or was it just outside of that context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on memory, a Serb soldier was driving from Prijedor to Ljubija. He pulled over and picked up a civilian, a hitchhiker. He admitted all that during proceedings. He asked him if he had any money, and the passenger said that he had 500 German marks. As far as I can remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you mind to focus your answer on my question. My question was whether it was in a military context. Was he driving to his family or was he with his unit or -- when it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the year. It may have been 1994. He was on his way back from the unit, as far as I can remember. It's very hard to remember all the details. Everything happened 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if I understand you well, it's not your recollection that it was in the direct military context that this crime was committed. I'm asking you this for the following reason. Because, Mr. Stojanovic, we have now listened to some now 40 minutes all kind of abstract matters. The charges in this case are, among others, that no investigations were initiated in relation to the crimes which are at the core of this case, and at the core of this case is not one specific murder of a civilian who is robbed from his properties; but it is war crimes, crimes against humanity. Do you remember a prosecution of any of the servicemen who was suspected of having committed a war crime, a crime against humanity, in the context of this indictment? And if you are not familiar with the indictment, it is about large-scale operations, shelling civilians, et cetera, that kind. Was there any prosecution to your knowledge initiated for such crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I arrived and joined the military prosecutor's office in late 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not interested in when you arrived. I'm interested in whether you ever prosecuted such a case. And, of course, I do understand that you didn't prosecute cases before you arrived in the prosecutor's office. That goes without saying. Do you remember any such case being prosecuted by you or your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember some cases. One of them would be Sugic, another Amidzic, and some others. In any case, there were many cases that were prosecuted by my colleagues. I can't really say what cases they prosecuted. But one thing I can say: Towards the end of the war - i.e., as the war drew on and the military prosecutor's office and the military court increased their capabilities - we started taking more and more such cases into consideration. You know that there is no statute of limitation on such crimes, so they could be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all in the abstract. Give us one such an example you prosecuted. I do understand that you were not fully familiar with the cases prosecuted by your colleagues. But one of those cases you prosecuted that is a clear war crime, crime against humanity, you prosecuted, tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I can remember as I sit here today is that I was involved in the Sugic case. And there was another case, Amidzic, that was processed after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us about the Sugic case. Who was prosecuted, what was the result of the prosecution, what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That case was heard by the military court in Banja Luka. When the Sugic brothers were brought in, I was the prosecutor on duty. I was invited to be present during their interrogation. After the interrogation, I asked for the two of them to be remanded in custody. That may have been in 1996 or 1997. I'm sure that it was after the war. What happened to the case later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to know cases during the war, if you have any.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do -- one of the bigger cases was the Stanovic case that I have already mentioned; however, I can't remember any other names. There was the Valter case but that's something different, not what you want me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not interested in the cases which are not covered by my question. But I do understand that the Stanovic case was then one which is covered by my question. Tell us, who was the accused, what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you properly, you're asking me about that first case, about the incident that happened on the Ljubija-Prijedor road?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm -- I'm interested in cases clearly dealing with war crimes, crimes against humanity, prosecuted during the wartime because the indictment charges that no effective action was taken either to prevent or to punish such crimes. So apart from who was driving what car and in what location prosecutor's office A was or prosecutor's office B was, or whether you had enough typewriters or not, I'd like to know what prosecutions were undertaken by your office during the war concerning crimes as they are charged in the indictment against the accused. That's what I'm, first of all, interested to hear from you, because that might challenge the Prosecutor's case. Any examples of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any such cases or examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. And, Mr. Stojanovic, I hope you understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honour, because those were questions -- of course, Your Honour. I had all those questions before me. I won't take up much more time, because you -- in practical terms, you have snatched my questions from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you took 40 minutes to tell us all -- to ask the witness about the system, about the cars driven, about whatever, but you didn't touch upon the core of the issue which is before this Court, and that's the reason why I put a few questions. And I now understand that this witness cannot tell us anything about any prosecution he was involved in during the wartime concerning crimes as they are charged against the accused you are defending at this moment. Therefore, that other knowledge may turn out not to be that relevant if we do not have information that really would assist the Chamber; that is, what action was taken in order to investigate and prosecute the crimes which are found in the indictment. And that's the reason why I thought after 40 minutes where you had only a few minutes left that perhaps I would try to get to the core of what this case is about. Please proceed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, this witness has clearly stated what was the legal framework and what were the possibility of conducting trials during that period. That's one reason. And the second is what we want to hear from this witness, and I will have a few more questions for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the cases Radulj [sic] and Amidzic. Can you remember what crimes were at stake and in what area. They were members of a group, a whole group that was charged, can you remember that case and what it was all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am very sorry. Just for the transcript. My friend is recorded to have referred to the cases "Rado and Amidzic," and I wonder if the first name might have been misrecorded. I heard the witness refer to the Amidzic case but not to a Rado case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we will put the question to the witness again after the break, Mr. Stojanovic, because we take the break first. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes, Witness. And then, Mr. Stojanovic -- You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how much time would you still need after the break, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, tell us, you mentioned the Amidzic case, could you please recall the charges against the accused, including Amidzic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Amidzic case was assigned to me sometime in 1996 or 1997. Several deputies had left the military prosecutor's office, and the remaining cases were assigned to the rest of us who stayed with the prosecutor's office. When I looked at the cases, I noticed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please answer the question. The question was: What the charges were against the accused. Not when you took over the case, not why the others left, but what were the charges.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. As far as I can remember, it was a grave crime against civilians committed in an elementary school near Kljuc. What I remember is that there were ten or even more accused in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us about the Sugic case? What crimes did they commit and what were they charged with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the Sugics murdered civilians in a village near Celinac. It happened either in 1992 or 1993. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1996 or 1997, when you were a deputy military prosecutor, were there any pressures put on you not to prosecute cases of Serbs committing crimes against non-Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no pressures either then or before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we move to the pressures. What explained that crimes committed in 1992 or 1993 were only prosecuted far later, five years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just share my opinion with you, if that may be of any use to you. I believe that the problem lies in the fact that the accused were not accessible, in the fact that there was not enough evidence, in the fact that many of the perpetrators got killed during the war or had left the territory of Republika Srpska; i.e., Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm more interested in facts than in opinions, but at least you gave some what may have been facts underlying what happened. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could a person be tried if you were not in a position to secure evidence, witnesses, facts due to the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, again, if you have no evidence, you can't prosecute someone. If wartime can -- I mean, that's all self-explanatory. Of course, what this Chamber needs is clear evidence. At least that's what we expect to receive during the Defence case, clear evidence that where the Prosecutor claims that not for good reasons matters were not investigated or prosecuted, that you'd tell us that not in general terms that if there's no evidence but why in those cases there really was no evidence, et cetera, rather than general statements. So could you please try to get to the concrete questions so that we can get concrete information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's be concrete. In the Amidzic case, could you prosecute if there were reasons that you mentioned in your answer to Judge Orie's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not if you can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not if there were reasons. Were there such reasons? What was the evidence available, why was that considered to be insufficient, who were the accused, were they inaccessible, et cetera? Not if they were inaccessible or if there was no evidence, that's of course -- these are all hypothetical questions. Let's get to the concrete facts of this or any other case where it would be in the interest of the Defence to demonstrate that everything was done that could be done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, in the Amidzic case, as a prosecutor, did you think that conditions were in place for you to prosecute at the moment when you took over the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I did what I could. I asked for the investigation to go on. Before the investigation was over, I could not do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the military prosecutor's office disbanded, including the military judiciary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an act which was passed in 2000 to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The cases which were not finalised and were within the jurisdiction of the military judiciary, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the cases falling under the jurisdiction of the military jurisdiction were forwarded to the civilian jurisdiction pursuant to special rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me finish with the following question: Do you know if the civilian judiciary continued to prosecute war crimes that happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that after that all the cases of crimes that happened from 1992 onwards are still being prosecuted in the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radulj. Thank you for your help. We have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Stojanovic. The Amidzic case, Witness, when did you take that over? I think you said. Was it in 1996, 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stojanovic asked you whether you could prosecute it then and you said I asked for the investigation to go on. But in this case, it's of primary importance to know whether it could be prosecuted in 1992, 1993, because this case is not about failure of doing what authorities had to do after the war but is mainly about failure to do what was necessary immediately sequential to the crimes being committed. Do you have any facts, to your knowledge, why or whether the Amidzic case could not be prosecuted or further investigated in 1992, 1993? Do you have any facts, to your knowledge, what was investigated in 1992 and 1993? And I'm interested in concrete facts, not in general opinions about that these kind of things are difficult in wartime because that goes without saying, but I'm asking you whether you have any concrete facts in that context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say what I heard; that is to say, what I learned. And I learned that when I came to the prosecutor's office in 1993. People were talking about a grave crime near Kljuc. I found out that some persons who were brought into custody by the military police but that, allegedly, the entire brigade had threatened to leave the position, or some soldiers had come before the military court and exerted pressure in that way to have these individuals released. These are just stories that I had heard. It's not that I saw any of this or that I was an eye-witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if earlier you said that you thought that the problems lie in the fact that the accused were not available and the fact that there was not evidence, that the one example you give us now is that the accused or the suspects were arrested but that there was a kind of a revolt and that that prevented, at least that's what you heard, the investigation and the prosecution to be continued. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said what I had heard, but allegedly only two persons were in custody, and there were more than ten suspects who were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at least those two were available. Because in your opinion you expressed earlier, no reference whatsoever was made to accused or suspects that were available, and you didn't hint in any way at what you heard about pressure put upon you not to prosecute, and even a kind of a revolution within the army where, as you're telling us now, that this is what you heard. So I'm wondering why your opinion you expressed a while earlier doesn't say anything about what you tell us now. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an explanation. I was answering questions that pertained to the period when I was in the prosecutor's office, and I spoke about that period. I thought that what had happened before that is something that I could not testify about, because I wasn't present when that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you were not present when happened what you just described and a moment ago you said you were expressing opinion rather than fact. I leave it to that. Mr. Traldi, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Radulj, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You find Mr. Traldi to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can I take it that your position is you told the truth in that interview?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to start just by following up briefly on the questions that you've been asked about the Banja Luka military court. First, have I understood correctly your testimony just now, that the evidence you gave about the Banja Luka military court and military prosecutor's office earlier refers only to the period after you joined the office in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand what you were saying, but I think that you're asking me to confirm that my statement pertains to the period from October 1993 when I was in the public prosecutor's office, if that is what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You've understood me correctly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, talking about testimony and talking about statements, let's clearly try to distinguish between the evidence given now and whatever appears in the statement the Chamber is unaware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me ask very precisely, as I referred to "evidence." Have I understood correctly your testimony that the evidence you've given this morning, in your testimony, about the Banja Luka military court and military prosecutor's office, refers only to the period after you'd joined the office in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you referred to two cases just now, the Amidzic case and the Sugic case. Both of those cases involved VRS soldiers accused of murdering Muslim civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You became involved with both of them in 1996, you said? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you would have reviewed the case files when you got assigned to the cases; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you would have heard discussion of the cases in the office as you testified about the Amidzic case; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you're aware as you sit here today that in 1992, shortly after those crimes happened, all of the perpetrators were arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, as you sit here today, you know that shortly after the crime that Amidzic and the others were charged with, they were arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I found out that only two perpetrators had been arrested - had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's go step by step. You don't recall from the case file that all 12 of the accused perpetrators gave statements confessing to the crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I do not remember because it was more than 20 years ago, and basically I didn't even review the entire case file then because the investigation hadn't been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so you also don't recall that they then wrote to General Talic complaining about their detention, that there was nothing in the case file for the next nine months after that, and that then two of them were rearrested in 1993? You don't remember that either?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only remember that somebody, maybe an investigating judge, this was already in 1996, said that most of them got killed. Not all of them, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you'd known about the crime already in 1992; right? About the massacre at Velagici school that they were arrested for and then released for.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard people talking about that in 1993, when I arrived in the prosecutor's office. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, you heard about it in Prijedor in 1992 even though it happened in Kljuc; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as Prijedor is concerned, I heard about that. But I'm repeating again that about Kljuc I learned in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's have 65 ter 32564, page 41. And this will be part of your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile ask one additional question. If you're assigned to a case, if the investigation is not complete, you just don't read the whole file? Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not that I don't read it. Since it is a request for investigation, then you have very little material to read. Very little can be seen from that material. It's only the very beginning of the investigation, and you have a great deal of files to deal with. So we had to move very quickly. And now it's been a very long time since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then just go back to your answer where you said you had not -- one second, please. You said: "... and basically, I didn't even review the entire case file then because the investigation hadn't been completed." I understood that you didn't review it. That means that you didn't read it. But if there is anything -- if you meant something else, then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I read the criminal report and the description of the crime. The number of victims, place, time, all of that. As for all the other details, at that moment I thought they were of lesser importance. Maybe I even read it, but right now I cannot remember. This is what I remains in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider confessions, as to what Mr. Traldi alluded to, by suspects who are detained to be less important if you take over a case file? I'm just asking you as a professional, whether you say it's of lesser importance that those detained are confessing to the crimes, that that's less important than what you did read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, confessions in a case like this are the most important. There is no denying that. But I'm saying that I may have read it, but after 23 or -4 years, I cannot recall the details. On the other hand, we had a large number of cases. I reacted immediately. I wanted the investigation to continue. First of all, I was surprised that the case had come to me. I asked for an urgent reaction then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've answered my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a portion of your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. The transcript is only in English, so I'm going to read to you slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could scroll to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could verify: Do you -- I noticed that you greeted me in the English language and only after that you said "dobro jutro" so may I take it that you can read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry. [Interpretation] I'm sorry, my English is not all that good. It is better to go through interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that we should not go. But if you read it on the screen, at least you have an opportunity to at least decipher some of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, I was asking you whether you'd heard about the Velagici massacre in 1992 when you were in Prijedor. And starting here, the third question up from the bottom, you're asked: "Do you recall when you first picked up the phone what that -- that's not the question -- when did you first pick up the Velagici file and how did it come into your hands if Captain Jovicinac didn't assign it to you?" You say: "I think it was the first time it actually came into my hands in 96 when I did react and when I did this proposal, by I did know about it prior to that, before that, because I heard stories." And you're asked: "When did you first hear about the Velagici massacre?" And you answered: "I think at the time I was still in Prijedor because it was an event people talked about." You're asked: "So, the Velagici massacre occurred the 1st of June 1992, was it soon after that, sometime in June 1992 when you heard about it?" Now, you describe that you first heard about a column of JNA vehicles that was attacked in May 1992 in Kljuc. And then turning to the next page at the top, you say: "... only later on, mid-June or mid-July did I hear about this massacre in the school, or the, Velagici is the name of the village. I only saw the case file in 96." So do you stand by what you said in your interview, that you were aware of the Velagici massacre in mid-June or mid-July 1992 when you were still in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you quite frankly, in view of the time distance involved, I believed that I knew about this even in Prijedor, as I stated then in 2002. As I've already said, it's been a long time and there is the effect of that. But I believe that what I stated then is correct, that I did have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it's correct that your recollection was fresher in 2002 than it is today, of course; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [In English] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this Velagici case was the only case in the Banja Luka military court where charges were initially brought under Article 142, war crimes, rather than under Article 36 for murder; right? And, sorry, I should be more specific. It's the only case where charges were brought against VRS soldiers under Article 142 for a crime against non-Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that it is a very, very serious crime. A grave crime. But at this moment, I cannot say how it was dealt with in legal terms. It is possible that it was Article 142.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, you were asked about Article 142 in your interview, and you stated that the military prosecutor had told you he received an instruction not to use Article 142, the qualification of war crimes, anymore. Do you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're putting me in a difficult situation. I cannot recall these details, but I can provide an opinion that was prevalent then among us lawyers, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm asking specifically whether you stand by your statement in your interview - and we can look at the full text, if it will help - that the military prosecutor told you he had received an instruction not to use the Article 142 classification for crimes by VRS soldiers against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind that statement 13 years ago, I believe that what I stated then is correct. Otherwise, I do not recall these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I take it you don't recall today whether he told you who gave him this instruction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what he said to me, I think that he did not say who it was that had given the instruction. However, if you allow me, why was it not qualified as a war crime? The only reason was because a state of war had not been declared at the time in Republika Srpska; rather, an imminent threat of war had been declared. So that is the reason why these crimes were not qualified as war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get a clarification. If they were not qualified as war crimes, why were they being brought before a military court and not taken to a civil court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer lies in the law itself; that is to say, military persons are held responsible for all the crimes they had committed regardless of whether these crimes are against the military or general crimes. In all of these cases, these were serious cases of murder and they could have been punished by the death sentence according to the law that was then in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do I understand then that even where a state of war has not been declared, if a soldier commits a murder of a civilian out there, that it comes to a military court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall provide an answer. He is brought before a military court because he is a member of the armed forces, a member of the army. It is on that basis that he is brought before a military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You had answered me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, clearly the Sugic brothers and the Velagici perpetrators weren't sentenced to terms of imprisonment for their crimes during the war. You agreed during your interview that had they been, they and others like them, it would have been a huge step to preventing other crimes that had happened that were committed by VRS soldiers during the war. Do you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that that would have been prevention and also it would have been educational, as it were, for others not to do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And not sentencing them sent the opposite message; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the prosecutor's office took the decision that -- well, let me start that question again. There was pretty efficient prosecution during the war of Serb soldiers who killed Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were prosecuted the same way as others. I did not see any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's have page 44 of this same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was not whether you see any difference. The question was, first of all, whether there was an efficient prosecution during the war of Serb soldiers who killed Serbs. Was there or was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to say that there was a difference there. The only difference may lie in the fact that it was easier to obtain evidence when a Serb was killed. If non-Serbs were killed, the victims and their relatives would have left and it was not as easy to obtain evidence that were needed for any kind of prosecution. When it came to Serb victims, it was easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is another portion of your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, and let's scroll back up a little bit so we start with "Because in Sanski Most ..." Now, you were asked similar questions in 2002 when your recollection was fresher. It was first put to you: "Because in Sanski Most no one got prosecuted for killing non-Serbs. At least, that's what it appears like, nobody ended up in prison." You responded: "Unfortunately that's correct, you're right." I'm going to stop there for a moment. Do you stand today by what you stated in your interview, that in Sanski Most nobody was prosecuted -- no VRS soldiers were prosecuted for killing non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your question takes me by surprise. I don't remember that anybody ever asked me about Sanski Most, nor do I have anything to do with Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a recording, audio, video, of this interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There is audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you say: "I didn't say it," then we'll just listen to the audio to find out whether what you're telling us now, that you have no recollection that any questions were asked about Sanski Most or that you said anything about it. If you -- if you seriously doubt that, then we should clearly find out whether an unfair record of your interview was prepared because this Chamber would not accept that. Do you insist on that you didn't say this and this wasn't asked? Because then we'll verify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't have any doubts. I do have doubts about my own memory, if I may be honest. Sanski Most is mentioned. I may have said that according to the records that were available to me at the time as a deputy prosecutor that nobody in Sanski Most was prosecuted. I can repeat that. Today, according to the records I had then, I can say still say that nobody in Sanski Most was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're moving from what we are doing. You're moving away from it. You're now saying: "I may have said something different from what is recorded," that you didn't tell it as what you remembered but that you learned that from the records. Now, apart from whether you did or not, and that's not the issue, if you say: "At the time, I didn't give my recollection but I told the interviewer that I had learned this from your records," then we'll check whether you said that or whether you said something different, whether you did or did not refer to the source of your knowledge. If you say: "I refer to the source of my knowledge and I didn't present it as my own recollection," then we'll verify it. If you think that it's worthwhile doing that, we'll do it. Do you want us to do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think that there is need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago you didn't have anything to do with Sanski Most. Now, of course, what you had to do with Sanski Most was that the 6th Brigade, based in Sanski Most, was part of the 1st Krajina Corps, and its soldiers and crimes they committed were within your office's jurisdiction; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking at the rest of your answer to this question, you say: "Yes, this is, you noted that, noticed very well because, ah, at the beginning of the war there were less, there were fewer cases processed, but the number grew as the war sort of developed because the bodies of authorities were being established, army became more and more disciplined. And they asked, they demanded responsibility for acts later on, the army demanded, but, as far as 1992 is concerned, everybody just wanted to forget everything about that." Now, first, when you said 1992, you were referring to a context of massive crimes committed by the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps again the Muslim and Croat civilian populations in their areas of responsibility during that time; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're then asked: "But, again, in large, in large part that was based on which nation the victim was from? Because we, if you agree with me, because we looked at nearly all of the murder files from 1992 to 1993. And there you will see pretty efficient prosecution of Serb soldiers who killed Serbs, usually family members. Would you agree?" And you answer: "That's correct because those, ah, cases had the precedents and those other cases were left for some other times when the political situation would be better, more friendly towards such cases." So two questions: First, when you say those other cases that were to be left for some other time, you're referring to a conscious decision not to prosecute VRS soldiers for crimes against Muslims and Croats during the war, even in the context of those massive crimes you just confirmed the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps were committing; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- I'm sure that you did not understand me properly. I never said, and nobody else did either, that perpetrators of war crimes should not be prosecuted. That certainly has never been said. Second of all, at the initial period, we did not have the necessary institutions that would have been able to prosecute criminals. All those things happened within the vacuum between the disappearance of the old state and the emergence of a new state. It also happened partly due to the political situation and the morale that prevailed in the army. There was a period of waiting for the institutions to be set up and that's when all the war crimes would be prosecuted, because there is no statute of limitations on them. In other words, nobody ever said that perpetrators of war crimes should not be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. First -- and I'm going to break it up into a few parts. First, do you stand by what you said in your interview, that it's correct that the records reflect pretty efficient prosecution of Serb soldiers who killed Serbs in the Banja Luka military court during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with that even today. That may be due to the translation. That was never my opinion. I still cannot say that I think that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if there is any translation issue, we'll check on the basis of the audio. We'll have the translation verified. If you didn't say it, we want to know because then we are presented with an inaccurate record of transcript of an interview. And in similar cases, it has turned out, now and then, that there were inaccuracies either in the recording or in the translation. What this Chamber, however, does not accept, that someone withdraws from his own words, blaming transcribers or interpreters for it rather than to acknowledge that that's what they said before. Therefore, again, the question here: Do you want us to verify the interpretation of your words spoken at the time? Say "yes" and we'll do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you do not challenge the accuracy of the recording of this statement, neither the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not challenging the accuracy, but I would like to provide an explanation. Please allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the only thing we were focusing on at this moment is what you said at the time. That matter has been resolved. I leave it in the hands of Mr. Traldi what other questions to put to you. And if your explanations are directly related to the question, then, of course, you have an opportunity to give such explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat my initial question: Do you stand by what we've now agreed you said in your interview, that it's correct that there was pretty efficient prosecution of Serb soldiers who killed Serbs in your court during the war? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, do you stand by what you said, that those cases, cases where are the victims were Serbs, had precedence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you also stand by, yes or no, what you said in your interview that other cases, which I take to mean cases where the victims were not Serbs, were left for some other time? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to provide an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the interpreters didn't hear your answer. So could you please first repeat your answer whether those cases against non-Serbs were left for some other time. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question please, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the fact that cases involving crimes by VRS soldiers against non-Serbs were left, at best, for some other time, to the point that you picked up a file in 1996 where the perpetrators of a mass murder had been arrested, confessed, and then been sent back to their units in 1992, reflects that what you said in 2002 in your interview was true - cases involving crimes against Serbs had the precedence; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cases against Serbs that had precedence concerned evading a military service. That's what I had in mind when I said that. Those were the only cases that fell into that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, in fact, there were successful prosecutions of soldiers for killing Serbs. The Pero Marin case; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that case at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, I'd put to you that what the records reflect is cases where the victims were Serbs or cases where, as you mentioned, the interests of the army were implicated, those cases not only had precedence in terms of successful prosecutions and sentences to terms of imprisonment, those cases came first, last, and only in the work of the Banja Luka military court. That's the truth, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the time for a break. I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I nevertheless would like to go to your statement in more detail and try to find out what you're telling us. As you can see on your screen, the question about the cases and which you said which cases had precedence, that question was exclusively about murder cases, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember those details. It was a long time ago. But I know for sure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read -- could you then read -- I'll slowly read it to you, the whole of what you said. The interviewer asked you: "... in large part, that was based on which nation the victim was from? Because we, if you agree with me, because we looked at nearly all the murder files from 1992 to 1993. And there you'll see pretty efficient prosecution of Serb soldiers who killed Serbs, usually family members. Would you agree?" I first -- I was seeking whether you agree that this question is clearly and exclusively about murder cases. Is it, or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer by just saying "yes" or "no." I've already asked you to allow me to explore. It was much easier to obtain evidence if both parties were Serbs because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That I may all be true. That's a different matter. You are interpreting your own answer, and for that reason I first take you to the question in order to see exactly what the question was about. There may have been good reasons for it, that's a different matter, but is this question purely about murders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, the answer would be yes, in view of my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I'll take you to your answer. Your answer is: "That's correct ..." And then on your own initiative, you continued: "... because ... those cases had the precedence and those other cases were left for some other times." Now, I think you explained to us a few minute ago that when you were referring to cases that had precedence that you were referring to those cases where not meeting your military obligations was concerned, whereas I have difficulties in understanding this answer in any other way than the cases that had the precedence is the cases of prosecutions of Serb soldiers killing Serbs and not by desertion or not responding to a call-up. That's my analysis of the words you used. If you have a good explanation as why I should understand your answer, I'm not talking about anything else but about your answer. If you have any explanation why where you said those cases had the precedence, how we should understand that as referring to desertion or not responding to call-ups, withdrawing from your military obligations, please tell us how we could possibly understand that in the way you now present it to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have completely confused me. I would like to see my signature on that text that I authored in 2002. This resembles an answer of a military judge, not a military prosecutor. I really don't understand. I'm totally confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you challenging the accuracy of the transcript and the interpretation, is that what you're doing? You know there is a standing offer, we'll verify it. But earlier, you started explaining that cases that had precedence were other cases, apparently explaining your explanation -- your statement, and I had difficulties in logically following that explanation. Therefore, I gave you this opportunity to logically explain how we could have possibly understood the reference to those cases that had precedence as anything else than murder cases, and you still have an opportunity to do that. If you take that opportunity, fine. You can do it. If you limit yourself to questioning the accuracy of this transcript and the interpretation, fine as well. Then we'll verify it. Which of the two: Do you want to further explain this text, not what happened, but this text; or do you want the accuracy to be verified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I have the right to ask for a break, please? Or shall I just wait for our regular break time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, do not -- Mr. Mladic, you do not have to interfere. It is regular break time, but if you could briefly answer my question whether you want to explain or whether you want the verification, then we'll do that after the break. We'll give you an opportunity after the break -- if you want to explain and if you want to challenge the accuracy, tell us now because we'll do it as soon as we can. Which of the two do you want to do after the break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I use the break time to give the whole thing a thought, please? And then I will be prepared to give you answer after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher. And we'll take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, we left you with a question before the break; that is, whether you wanted to have the accuracy of the recording to be verified, or whether you would like to give an explanation on the context in which you used the words "those cases had the precedence" as referring to anything else than to murder cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a good and long thought about everything. I provided that statement 13 years ago, which is why I don't remember many things, so I won't challenge the statement. I don't want it to be verified. Nothing would happen as a result of that. Nothing would be changed. And as for the question about prosecuting crimes where, as you put it, Serbs took precedence over others, I stand by my statement that at that moment I had in mind crimes concerning the military and military service. Exclusively that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not really an explanation because that was clear already, but I leave it in Mr. Traldi's hands how to proceed. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd actually intended to turn to a different topic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm going to take you now back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 07108.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, what we see on the screen, so far only in the B/C/S, is the decision appointing you as the acting public attorney in May of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Where was your office?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My office was on the second floor of the building housing the Prijedor basic court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How far was that from the Prijedor SJB, the police station?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station was very close. In the same street. In the neighbouring building on the right-hand side, if you were standing in front of the court building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the municipality building was across the street; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Also on the other side of the street, same block, same street, was the headquarters of the Ljubija mine company where you'd previously been employed; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we see in the same decision appointing you that Esad Mehmedagic is dismissed. Mr. Mehmedagic was a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And his vision was impaired; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you never saw him after the war; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
