utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has received evidence that Mehmedagic was held at Omarska in the summer of 1992, was taken out, never returned, and was later exhumed from the Stari Kevljani mass grave. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about that. I learned that he had been exhumed, but I don't know when. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you also learn he'd been held in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that he was in Omarska, but I did know that he had been taken from his house and taken somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you know who took him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you know what institution the people who took him were from; the police, the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mehmedagic was one of many Muslims and Croats who were dismissed from their jobs in Prijedor municipality in May of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You and the president judge of the court, Judge Mico Kreco, agreed when you spoke about these dismissals that they were unlawful and unreasonable; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Like you, Judge Kreco was a Serb by ethnicity; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, there had been a different president judge of the court previously, a Nedzad Seric; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't know him. But, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Omer Kerenovic had previously been a judge on the Prijedor court, right, before the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Also a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Both Judge Seric and Judge Kerenovic were also exhumed from the Stari Kevljani mass grave after the war; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So are you also not aware that they were also detained in Omarska beforehand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mehmedagic, Judge Seric, Judge Kerenovic, they were prominent people in the community in Prijedor before the war; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Other prominent Muslims were killed in the camps too, right, like the mayor, Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You heard he was held in Omarska and he was killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yesterday, at transcript page 35488, you discussed your view that in 1992 the organs of power in Bosnia had disappeared and it was necessary to create new organs. Now, the removal of these community leaders, these prominent Muslims, was one way that the organs of power in Prijedor disappeared or were transformed; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the new organs of power included the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In Prijedor, the new organs of power included the Prijedor Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You testified a moment ago that you and Judge Kreco agreed the dismissals of Muslims and Croats were illegal. Those dismissals went ahead anyway because it was these new Bosnian Serb organs of power that were really making the decisions, that were really in charge of life in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that they were really the ones who were in charge of life. Maybe individuals made decisions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff made a decision that Muslims and Croats should be fired. The view of the public attorney, the view of the presiding judge, was that this was illegal. The Muslims and Croats were fired anyway. That's because the Crisis Staff had the power; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that on the 29th or 30th of April there was a change of government, but only top people were replaced. So that was done in April. Not the other non-Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: People in companies were replaced in May and June of 1992; right? Non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So not just the top people in government. People throughout the society, particularly in positions of authority - Muslims and Croats, were dismissed from their jobs; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the dismissals came after the units of the Republika Srpska Army were being formed. Those who did not accept that left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, just looking at this particular example, we see Mr. Mehmedagic was dismissed as of the 4th of May. That's a couple of days after the take-over and even before the VRS was formed; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we discussed a moment ago, and you confirmed, what happened to a number of prominent Muslims in the community. That would have had a devastating effect on the Muslim community in Prijedor, the death and disappearance of many prominent figures; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that interethnic relations in Prijedor had been good before the war. Prijedor was known, in fact, before the war, as a place where interethnic relations were good, a place where the old communist slogan of brotherhood and unity really meant something; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 01078.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when you say new organs of power had to be created, Yugoslavia, as it had been known, disappeared. What was destroyed was exactly that place where interethnic relations were good, that place where brotherhood and unity really meant something. That place effectively didn't exist anymore; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that sense, it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31035.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you confirmed a moment ago that Muslims and Croats were dismissed from companies, as well as jobs in government. One of the companies where the Muslim and Croat employees were dismissed in the late spring and early summer of 1992 was the Ljubija mine company where you'd previously worked; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report to SJB Prijedor by the Ljubija mine company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 3 in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, looking at the second paragraph, we read: "Immediately after the take-over of power on 30 April 1992, a clear differentiation of personnel was made in our enterprise ..." Now "differentiation" refers to what we've been talking about, differentiation along ethnic lines, the dismissals of Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we see immediately following that, that: "... after the attack on Prijedor on 30 May 1992," that you described yesterday, "a wartime staffing specification was introduced and personnel were assigned accordingly, in keeping with the decisions of the Government of Republika Srpska." Now, the decisions of the government of the Republika Srpska would have been relayed to this company through the regional Crisis Staff and the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do not remember that. I was in Brezicani the last time in September 1991. I did not return there after that, so I cannot say anything specific about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you are developing a speed of speech which is far too high.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll try and restrain it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, you're aware, putting the question somewhat differently, that the Muslims and Croats dismissed in Prijedor were dismissed because of a decision by the Prijedor Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we see at the bottom of the page and turning to the top of page 4 in B/C/S, a reference to the consistent implementation in this company of the decisions to dismiss workers of the Crisis Staff War Presidency of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly and the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And so the Ljubija mine company was implementing the Crisis Staff -- the Prijedor Crisis Staff and the autonomous region's Crisis Staff's decisions; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably it was that way if this document says so. I really have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning back to page 3 in both languages, we read below attachment 2 at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S that: "Already in early June, only around ten days after the fighting in the town, the army and police took over all direct securing of facilities, property, and persons. Additional measures were taken to ensure general security in the enterprise and very close co-operation was also continued with the Army Main Staff and the Public Security Centre." Now, you would have been aware, because you were next door to the public security station and across the street from your old employer's headquarters, you would have been aware that they were co-operating with the police and with the army; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that the building is close to my building doesn't mean that I have to know what is going on in that building. So what you are putting to me now is the first I've ever heard of it. I cannot confirm or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 5 in the English and 6 in the B/C/S, we see a list of high personnel in that company beginning with the acting director, Ostoja Marjanovic. You knew him, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you know that, as reflected here, he was, in 1992, acting director of the company and was mobilised in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now the resources of important companies, would they be mobilised at times for the war effort?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you know, of course, the Ljubija mine company was an important company in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ran three mines, employed large numbers of people.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Its resources were also put at the disposal of the war effort; right? Also mobilised.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Witness, I've one other question for you. When Mr. Traldi asked you whether in companies people were dismissed as well, you said there were such cases. Looking at this document, I see that only for the Ljubija mine it amounts to 1.500, if not more. I'm just wondering what you meant by "there were such cases" instead of perhaps saying that this happened on a massive scale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what was then done at the mine is something that I cannot know about. Among other things, the reason was that production had ceased and also probably because of the mass departure of non-Serbs from Prijedor. That kind of thing certainly happened, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that there is more to say about it, but to say there were such cases where it happened on a massive scale. And I take it it would not have escaped your attention that 1.500 - that's quite a large number - were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to give a brief explanation. When I said "individual cases," I meant what happened at the end of April, or rather beginning of May, when only people in top positions were being replaced; whereas, what happened after the 30th of May is a completely different story, and it is true that then there were mass dismissals of employees because everything bad that was done in Prijedor was done after the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say everything that was bad was done -- in Prijedor was done after the 30th of May, 1992. You know there was killing of large numbers of Muslims, destruction of large amounts of Muslim civilian property during operations in Hambarine and Kozarac before the 30th of May; right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, turning to some of those other bad things, you testified yesterday at transcript page 35504 that you had no contact with Omarska and Keraterm. You knew during your time as public attorney in Prijedor that people were being taken to Omarska and Keraterm, non-Serbs, and non-Serbs were being murdered and tortured in those camps; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You testified a moment ago about the mass departure of non-Serbs from Prijedor. Those were the people who yesterday you said were forced to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And one of the people who was held in Keraterm was a friend of yours named Islamovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he told you that he'd had to promise to leave Prijedor municipality, and when he did promise to do so he was released; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He asked for help as well, to leave Keraterm. So I helped him get out, indirectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you know that the Muslim and Croat places of worship in Prijedor town were destroyed in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One of the bad things that happened right on the 30th of May was that a mosque was destroyed; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And after the fighting that day, Muslims and Croats had to hang white flags from their houses; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not understand the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. You're being asked to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you discussed on direct examination your letter objecting to the occupation of abandoned houses, abandoned property. A lot of the property which was abandoned had previously belonged to people who'd been held in the camps; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, is it right that in your letter you did not at any point refer to the need to return the property to its rightful owners. You simply referred to the need to allow it to be allocated properly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of my letter was primarily to protect property, and I pointed out there that it has to do with private property which is inalienable, and that the municipality will be responsible if there is destruction of property in order to have this property preserved and returned to the owners one day. I said there that no one knows how long the war will last. One day it would have to come to an end, and one day people will come to get their own. And Dayton was written in that context, roughly, as far as the return of property is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, your letter was written in the context of a decision that had been taken a month earlier to declare abandoned property in Prijedor municipality the property of the state; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember. A temporary decision was taken; that is to say, that it is temporarily the property of the state so that it could be safe-guarded better. But it doesn't mean that it's owned by the municipality, and no one ever thought that it was supposed to be owned by the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And your letter makes it clear that the priority is allocating this abandoned property that's now property of the state to VRS soldiers and their families; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that property was supposed to be distributed to the families of the fallen soldiers and to people who were disabled during the war. At that time, many buses full of Serbs arrived from Travnik, Zenica, Sarajevo, and other places. So these refugees were supposed to be put up somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn back for just a moment to the take-over of Prijedor. At that time for the first time Radio Prijedor played Chetnik nationalist songs; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Prijedor from the 15th of April until the 15th of May, so I don't know about that period. After that, there were songs, among others, Serb national songs, including Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were asked in your interview whether it was announced at the time of the Prijedor -- sorry, the take-over of Prijedor that Prijedor was going to be called the Serb municipality of Prijedor. You explained that that wasn't necessary because Prijedor was part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and all of the municipalities within the ARK had Serb authorities, so you considered it logical that the authorities in Prijedor would be Serb authorities. Do you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That first part of the question, as far as this name "Serb Prijedor" is concerned, this is the first time I hear of it. And in relation to that, if there is a Serb autonomous region, then that was the region that was in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia, then there was no need to change the name of Prijedor, and then there are these authorities that are in favour of preserving Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's have quickly 65 ter 32564, page 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, can I ask one follow-up question. You explained your letter when asked by Mr. Traldi by saying that, of course, after the war would be over, Muslims would return to their homes and that's what all was to be expected. Now, that's not very explicit in that letter. And this Chamber has heard evidence that it may not have been on everyone's mind that Muslims who had left the territory in those municipalities were expected to return. We even have heard evidence which hinted at an expectation that they would not return and that was even intended, that they would not return. My question to you is: Apart from your implicit understanding of what the expectations were, could you point at any document or any specific fact in which it becomes clear that your assumption that non-Serbs would return to the areas which they had left was realistic and that was really what was expected to happen? So concrete points which would have expressed that, such as if, after the war, the Muslims will return, we should keep their homes ready for them or whatever. So I'm seeking concrete facts which would support what you describe, more or less, as an implicit assumption.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, allow me to answer this question. First of all, when I wrote the letter, after all, I'm a person who had a great deal of experience as a lawyer even then, and I was familiar with international law, and as a reserve officer I was familiar with the law of war, and I knew who in wartime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking that. I'm not asking on what your assumption was based. I'm asking you about concrete facts, and I just gave a possible example, concrete facts which would contradict some of the evidence this Chamber heard and which would be in support of your assumption.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the essence was to protect the privately owned property of Prijedor that belonged to the citizens who had left Prijedor. I believe I wasn't clear enough on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, I wish to indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've been perfectly clear on that. You told us that in very clear terms, but it's not an answer to my question. Do you have any minutes of meetings where it was explicitly discussed how Muslims would be helped to return, how to bring them back their property, et cetera? I mean, I'm asking you about concrete facts, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're looking for written evidence, I don't have any on me. However, later at the meetings of the municipal assembly, those issues were discussed. I left Prijedor after that, so I don't know what was going on. But there is one thing that I need to say: Property or assets did not fall into anybody else's hands. Whatever it was, it waited for its rightful owners to return, like everywhere else in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So Prijedor did not differ from other towns, such as Zenica, Bijeljina, Travnik, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last part, again, is not an answer to my question but apparently something you want to emphasize. I leave it to that. Mr. Traldi. Oh, Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that we don't interrupt you many times, Mr. Traldi. Sir, just want some clarification to one of your answers here. At page 50, lines 15, you were asked a question: "So not just the top people in government. People throughout the society, particularly in positions of authority - Muslims and Croats, were dismissed from their jobs; right?" You answered: "Yes. I think that the dismissals came after the units of the Republika Srpska Army were being formed. Those who did not accept that left." My question to you is: What is the significance of mentioning units of the Army of the Republika Srpska in relation to this question put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The significance of that lies in the fact that those units were replenished from the ranks of those who wanted to defend Republika Srpska and who wanted to live there. Those who didn't want to do so decided to leave Prijedor, so they resigned because there was no production, or certain companies drafted their own lists, and I suppose that the ethnic principle was used in drafting such lists, and those people were fired from their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're not answering my questions. You are telling the Court that the dismissal of people escalated after the VRS was formed. So I don't understand what you mean by "replenishing VRS soldiers," because they were not being dismissed from the army, they were being dismissed from their companies, and you say this happened after the units of the VRS had been formed. Am I to understand, if I may put it bluntly, that you are saying here that the escalation was there because the VRS was promoting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we spoke at cross-purposes here. I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you how you spoke. I'm just asking you whether this is what you meant. You volunteered VRS. There was no mention of VRS in the question. You volunteered the fact that this went up after the VRS units were formed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you saying "no" to? Are you saying you didn't volunteer the VRS name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I may have mentioned the VRS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did mention --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- by accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did mention it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 30th of May, after the attack on Prijedor, there was a large-scale dismissal from companies of non-Serb workers. And if I had mentioned the VRS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this happened, according to this statement that you have given, that happened after the formation of the VRS units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I would like to withdraw that from my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately you cannot, it's on the record. Thank you so much, Mr. Traldi. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just returning to the question of your view on the Serb nature of the authorities in the municipality within the ARK, you were asked a similar question to what I'd asked you in your interview, and you responded: "I don't remember the prefix 'Serbian,' but that is possible. This was a long time ago. I don't remember. I think it wasn't necessary to specially state that it was a Serbian municipality, because through that it didn't become the Member ... It was already now a member of The ARK." You were asked: "The Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina?" And you answered: "Yes." And you were asked: "What do you mean by that 'it became part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina'?" And you answered: "'Cause all the municipalities within the Autonomous Region of Krajina had Serbian authorities. It's just that the question that you asked whether it was a 'Serbian" or just 'The municipality of Prijedor.' You didn't have to say that it was Serbian, because it had become ... it was logical that all the municipalities which were part of the ARK would be Serb municipalities." And you added that you didn't think that the name had changed. Now, do you stand by that portion of your interview that I have read back to you as truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you'd heard that, speaking of the ARK, its Crisis Staff President, Radislav Brdjanin, referred to Muslims as balijas; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's a derogatory term for Muslims, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, finally, sir, yesterday you testified that the Ljubija mine company that you'd worked for owned three mines: The Ljubija, Omarska, and Tomasica mines. You confirmed earlier that you'd known that people were detained in terrible, criminal conditions on the Omarska mine property at the Omarska camp; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that non-Serbs were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that there were mass graves on the properties of both the Ljubija and Tomasica branches of the mine company. Were you also aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were rumours about Ljubija. I didn't know about Tomasica until perhaps a few months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, it was exhumed in 2013, so you've known for at least a year and a half; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? Are you referring to Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Tomasica, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, Tomasica. Ah, yes. What I meant was I have learnt about that only recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So your evidence is you weren't aware of that mass grave until after the war, long after the war; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so you were never, as a military prosecutor, directed to investigate either the creation of the grave or the murders of the people who were buried there, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Stojanovic, we'll take a break. Could you tell us how much time you would need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than ten minutes, Your Honour. I need to cover three different topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break first. Mr. Radulj, you're invited to follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes because we will resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you remind Mr. Mladic and tell him how to behave in the court, also in relation to the public gallery. If you address him, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, you'll now be further examined by Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radulj, after the setting up of the VRS and after the mobilisation, could somebody who was not a member of the military or who did not have work obligation stay working in a company, irrespective of his or her position there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, all militarily able-bodied men had to be either in the military or they had to do work obligation. Therefore, there was no third option. I'm talking about militarily able-bodied people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If a militarily able-bodied man, a military conscript, did not respond to a mobilisation call and didn't want to defend the state, could he then be subject to criminal responsibility for not responding to that obligation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You already spoke about that as a case that had priority before a military judiciary. Why? Why would such cases enjoy priority before the military judiciary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those cases had priority in order to boost military discipline. On the other hand, complying with constitutional obligation on the part of every citizen meant that they had to serve in the army, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Ljubija mine, did people of Serb origin have to leave for the aforementioned reasons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irrespective of ethnic affiliation, those who did not respond to the call-ups had to be criminally charged or, rather, prosecuted or they were investigated, and that applied to Serb citizens as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up P7385. I believe that I'm interested in page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a while ago we had an occasion to see it when the Prosecutor asked you about that document. Do you remember the document that you have before you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, I'm interested in the following page, please, and in the English version I believe that we are on the page that I'm interested in. Let's go to the following page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown one part of this report; inter alia, you were asked about that. It says here of the total number of 4.297 employees, 1.887 were dismissed during the first differentiation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading in the English, Mr. Stojanovic? I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- yes, that's correct, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now follow me? 1.887 were dismissed. After the legally prescribed procedure had been conducted, 216 appeals of workers whose appeals were valid and grounded as shown by the attached documents were held, or better put accepted. After subsequent checks, another 74 workers were dismissed, including 16 Serbs who had left the territory of Republika Srpska of their own volition. In other words, the emphasis is put here on the reasons why Serbs were dismissed. When it says that they left the territory of Republika Srpska of their own volition, what did they -- what did that imply, Mr. Radulj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the prosecutor's office, we considered such cases as a departure in order to evade military service, if those people were military conscripts, and we found those cases interesting. As for other cases and departure for other reasons, that was not subject of our work at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask you this: If somebody left their town and the company that they worked for, if they didn't turn up for work for no reason at all and for a certain time, could they be kept in employment according to the then-prevalent laws?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the prevalent laws said that if an employee was absent from work for five consecutive days without a justified reason was summarily dismissed, and I believe that we are talking about that kind of cases. I suppose that that is the case because I didn't read the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I will finish with another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just intervene for one moment. You earlier confirmed the differentiation referred to, differentiation along ethnic lines, the dismissals of Muslims and Croats. Now, if you say: "I suspect that that was, I've not read the whole of the document, there must have been other reasons as well," you confirmed the differentiation is ethnic differentiation, and what is written here is about what happened in the context of this differentiation. Therefore, I am putting this to you that if you now suggest that there may have been other reasons not having read the document, that the document is about dismissals on the basis of the differentiation as was instructed, and that is, I think, differentiation. So if you want to say, well, there were other reasons to dismiss people as well, fine, may be the case, but that's not what this document is about. And since you were wondering whether you had sufficiently read the document to make any comments, I just am explaining to you now how the words are used in this document so as to give you an opportunity to comment on that use of language in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've not seen this document before, i.e., the question based on the document that was put to me by the Prosecutor. But now that the Defence lawyer has read the document to me and when he has put the question to me, and I realised that there were Serbs that were also dismissed, I know that there were such cases. However, when I answered the Prosecutor's questions, I spoke about the large majority of non-Serbs who failed to respond to call-ups, inter alia, but there were others as well as you can see from this report issued by the Ljubija mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I have a little follow-up here. The 16 Serbs that were said to be dismissed were dismissed because they left of their own volition. What would be the point of keeping them on the payroll if they are not coming to work? In fact, they seemed to have resigned rather than being dismissed. Thank you. So that cannot be the answer. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Radulj, I would like to take you to page 41, lines 11 through 19, of today's record. You were asked whether the cases of non-Serb victims were delayed for some other time, and you said yes. I would like to ask you why were those cases left for later? Why were they prosecuted only later, not at the moment when they happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must emphasize that nobody ever issued a document or a decree for those cases to be left for later. It was down to the situation. There were priorities, and those priorities involved the military-related cases. I've already spoken about that. It was virtually impossible to secure evidence that would have made it possible to have lawful proceedings in those cases. Neither the prosecutor's office nor the court had enough staff or equipment in order to do things properly at the time. Later, when things improved somewhat, those cases were dealt with one by one. Those proceedings are still ongoing at various courts all over Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, on behalf of the Mladic Defence, I would like to thank you. We have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Stojanovic. Do you have any further questions, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. First, can we have 65 ter 32447. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document coming from the military prosecutor's office attached to the army Main Staff entitled: "Dispatch on the Institution of Criminal Proceedings Against Persons Who Have Not Responded to the Call-up Or Left Units Without Authorisation."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 5, end of the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We see its sent to the various military prosecutor's offices. It's correct that the priority -- that one of the priorities was dealing with prosecuting people who didn't respond to the call-up and that that priority was set by the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before. It was never shown to me. I see it for the first time here. As far as I can see, it was drafted in the month of the September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in office at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. What it reflects, though, is the priority that you mentioned on redirect, the priority of cases involving not responding to a call-up being passed from General Gvero to the various military prosecutor's offices; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7386, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And finally if we could have 65 ter 32564, page 46. I see I've been recorded to say "23564" and I'd meant to say 32564. If we could scroll to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You're being asked about your work in the military prosecutor's office, and you're asked a question about criminal law, both procedural and substantive. You're asked whether: "... it would be possible for a deputy military prosecutor, a prosecutor to obtain a conviction in a case... where the accused gave a full confession to the military prosecutor and the investigative judge, so a proper formal statement that included a confession? To the crime of murder?" Just to summarises it briefly, Mr. Resch asks or identifies other available evidence: "The victims' bodies and ballistic tests confirming the bullets that killed the body came from the accused person's gun and asks: "Under those circumstances, without a statement from the victim's family whether he can get a conviction." And if we turn to the next page. There is a lengthy discussion about the procedure of the case, and if we scroll to the middle of the page, summarising your answer, Mr. Resch says: "The fact that the relatives did not testify would not preclude a finding of guilty." Your answer: "What do you mean by wouldn't preclude?" He says: "Prevent, prevent ..." And you say: "I think there are no legal obstacles to him being pronounced guilty," which I take to mean the accused person in the circumstances that were described. So do you stand today by your answer in your interview that where the victim's body is available, the murder is confessed, ballistic tests confirm the murder weapon, the legal obstacles that you mentioned on redirect would not have prevented a conviction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on everything that I heard from you, I don't see a reason why a conviction should not be pronounced. So, yes, I adhere by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Radulj, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, a long way for you, and very having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and were put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again, and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some time left. We'll deal with some very practical matters. I'd first like to deliver two decisions and that may consume all the time which is left. The first is a decision the Chamber will now deliver on the expertise of Svetlana Radovanovic with regard to her analysis of Prosecution expert reports authored by witnesses Ewa Tabeau and Helge Brunborg. On the 9th of February of this year, the Defence filed a notice of disclosure of Svetlana Radovanovic's expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution responded on the 11th of March, submitting that while it does not challenge the expert status of Radovanovic or the relevance of her report, it also does not accept the conclusions of the report and therefore requests to cross-examine her. On the 25th of March, the Defence filed a response to the Prosecution's 11th of March submission. On the 1st of April, the Prosecution sought leave to reply and filed its reply to the Defence response. The Chamber will address the 25th of March and the 1st of April submissions in a separate decision. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October 2012 decision concerning Expert Witness Richard Butler. On the basis of Radovanovic's curriculum vitae and considering that the Prosecution does not dispute Radovanovic's qualifications as an expert in the field of demographics, the Chamber is satisfied that she has specialised knowledge and expertise and that such knowledge and expertise may be of assistance to the Chamber in assessing the expert evidence presented by the Prosecution during its case-in-chief. With regard to the Prosecution request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Defence plans to call Radovanovic to give evidence. The Prosecution will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine her. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides pursuant to Rule 94 bis that Witness Radovanovic may be called to testify as an expert witness and shall be made available for cross-examination by the Prosecution. The Chamber defers its decision on the admission of the report to the time of the witness's testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The next decision the Chamber will now deliver is its decision on the expertise of Dragic Gojkovic with regard to the destruction of the religious buildings in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995 and his analysis of the Prosecution expert report authored by Witness Andras Riedlmayer. On the 13th of February, 2015, the Defence filed a notice of disclosure of Dragic Gojkovic's expert report, pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution responded on the 16th of March, submitting that while it does not challenge the expert status of Gojkovic, or the relevance of his report, it does not accept the report's conclusions and therefore requests to cross-examine him. The Prosecution further submits that 15 documents attached to the report should not be considered as a part of the report and that the Defence should seek leave to add them to its 65 ter exhibit list and tender them for admission separately. On the 30th of March, the Defence filed a response to the Prosecution's 16th of March submission. On the 7th of April, the Prosecution sought leave to reply and filed its reply to the Defence response. The Chamber will address the 30th of March and the 7th of April submissions in a separate decision. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October, 2012 decision concerning Expert Witness Richard Butler. On the basis of Gojkovic's curriculum vitae and considering that the Prosecution does not dispute Gojkovic's qualifications as an expert on destruction of religious buildings in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995, the Chamber is satisfied that he has specialised knowledge and expertise in that field and that such knowledge and expertise may be of assistance to the Chamber in assessing the expert evidence presented by the Prosecution during its case-in-chief. With regard to the Prosecution request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Defence plans to call Gojkovic to give evidence. The Prosecution will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine him. Concerning the Prosecution submissions related to 15 documents attached to the report, the Chamber invites the Defence to request their addition to its 65 ter exhibit list. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides pursuant to Rule 94 bis that Witness Gojkovic may be called to testify as an expert witness on destruction of religious buildings in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995 and shall be made available for cross-examination by the Prosecution. The Chamber defers its decision on the admission of the report to the time of the witness's testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. We have two minutes left. Let me just take one or two small items from the pending issues list. I start with remaining associated exhibits to Witness Vidoje Blagojevic's statement. On the 1st and the 2nd of April, the Chamber inquired whether the Defence's failure to address document bearing Rule 65 ter number 14584 during the testimony of Vidoje Blagojevic meant that it was withdrawn as an associated exhibit. The Chamber has not heard from the Defence on this matter and considers its silence to be an implicit withdrawal. The Defence has an opportunity to revisit the matter within three days. My last item deals with P7038. On the 21st of January of this year, the Chamber marked for identification under seal P7038 based on the Prosecution's submission that the whole document might not need to be admitted into evidence. This can be found at transcript page 30337. On the 2nd of April, the Prosecution informed the Chamber via an e-mail that the parties had discussed this issue and are in agreement that P7038 should be admitted in its entirety. Assuming that the Defence does not object, the Chamber hereby admits P7038 into evidence under seal. We'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 14th of May, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30 in the morning.
